questions.question: What data type does `xpath('//title/text()', doc)` return, even when only one node matches?
options: A plain text string
An `xml[]` array
A JSONB object
An integer count of matches
questions.explanation: `xpath()` always returns an `xml[]` array, never a scalar, because XPath expressions can match zero, one, or many nodes. To get a human-readable string you must index into the array (`[1]`) and cast it with `::text`, which surprises most learners expecting a plain string back on the first try.

questions.question: What is the relationship between `unnest()` and `array_agg()`?
options: They are unrelated aggregate functions
`unnest()` expands an array into rows; `array_agg()` collapses rows back into an array — they are inverses
`unnest()` only works on JSONB, `array_agg()` only works on arrays
`array_agg()` must run before `unnest()` in every query
questions.explanation: `unnest(tags)` is a set-returning function that turns a single array value into one row per element. `array_agg(col)` does the opposite: it aggregates multiple rows into a single array. Together they let you round-trip between the relational (row) and array representations of the same data.

questions.question: Why can't you enforce a foreign key on individual elements of an `int[]` column like `order_ids int[]`?
options: Postgres disables FK syntax on array-typed columns entirely
Postgres has no mechanism to validate each array element against another table's primary key — the array is just an opaque list of integers to the database
FK constraints only work with TEXT arrays
You can enforce it, but only with a BEFORE trigger, never a constraint
questions.explanation: A standard `FOREIGN KEY` constraint validates a single scalar column against a referenced table's key. Postgres has no built-in syntax to validate every element inside an array column the same way, so `order_ids int[]` can silently contain IDs for rows that were deleted or never existed. This is the core argument for using a junction table instead of an array whenever referential integrity matters.

questions.question: What happens when you try to insert a value not in an ENUM's defined list, e.g. `INSERT INTO person VALUES ('angry')` when `mood` only allows `'happy'`/`'sad'`?
options: Postgres silently coerces it to NULL
Postgres raises an error: invalid input value for enum
Postgres automatically adds the new value to the ENUM
The insert succeeds but the value is stored as text
questions.explanation: ENUMs enforce a fixed, closed set of allowed labels at the type level, so an out-of-list value is rejected outright with an 'invalid input value for enum' error. To allow the new value, you must explicitly run `ALTER TYPE mood ADD VALUE 'angry'` — this rigidity is the trade-off for the type's compactness (4-byte internal storage) and integrity guarantees.

questions.question: When should you choose a Composite Type over a JSONB column for structured data like an address?
options: Always — Composite Types are strictly better in every scenario
When the structure is fixed and known at design time and you want strong per-field typing; JSONB is better when the structure is variable, sparse, or evolves per-row without a migration
Never — JSONB always outperforms Composite Types
Only when the data needs to be queried with GIN indexes
questions.explanation: Composite Types give you compile-time-like guarantees: each field has a declared type (e.g., `zip text`) and the shape is consistent across every row, which is ideal when you know the schema in advance. JSONB trades that structure for flexibility — useful when different rows might have different fields or the shape changes over time without a `ALTER TYPE`/migration step.

questions.question: Which Postgres range-type operator checks whether two ranges (e.g., two booking time slots) overlap?
options: `@>` (contains)
`&&` (overlap)
`<@` (contained by)
`=` (equality)
questions.explanation: The `&&` operator returns true if two range values share any point in common, which is exactly the check a booking or scheduling system needs before confirming a new reservation. `@>` and `<@` instead test full containment (one range entirely inside or around another), which is a stricter and different condition.

questions.question: Why is `tsvector`/`tsquery` generally preferred over `LIKE '%pattern%'` for searching large text columns?
options: `LIKE` is faster but less accurate
`tsvector` stores a normalized, indexed list of word stems that can be searched efficiently via a GIN index, whereas `LIKE '%pattern%'` cannot use a standard B-Tree index and forces a full scan
`tsquery` only works on XML columns
There is no performance difference; it's purely a syntax preference
questions.explanation: A leading-wildcard `LIKE '%pattern%'` cannot use a standard index because the match could start anywhere in the string, forcing Postgres to scan every row. `tsvector` pre-processes text into normalized lexemes (word stems) that a GIN index can search directly via `@@` against a `tsquery`, making full-text search dramatically faster at scale.

questions.question: Can XML content be indexed in Postgres for fast querying?
options: No, XML can never be indexed
Yes, but only with GIN indexes like JSONB
Yes, using a functional index on the result of an `xpath()` expression cast to text
Only Oracle databases support indexing XML
questions.explanation: Postgres supports functional (expression) indexes, so you can index the *result* of a deterministic expression like `xpath('//title/text()', doc)::text` rather than the raw XML column itself. This lets a query filtering on that extracted value use an Index Scan instead of re-parsing the XML document on every row during a Seq Scan.
